title: Presses and papers
hookLine: Gurmukhi newspapers and presses spread the reform

cards: Ink on fingers. In a back room in Lahore, a typesetter picks small metal letters out of a wooden case, one by one, and lines them up in a frame.
They're Gurmukhi letters, the same shapes a reader meets on a page of the Granth. A lever comes down, the press clanks, and a sheet lifts off with the ink still wet.
Soon it will be folded, bundled, and carried to another town.

teach.b: First, the script. Gurmukhi is the alphabet the Gurus used for their hymns; tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping it for Sikh use.
To print in Gurmukhi was to print in the letters of the Granth, so a newspaper set in that type could double as a reading lesson for the scripture.
Second, the papers. Reformers started newspapers in Punjabi. The Khalsa Akhbar came out of Lahore, linked to the scholar Giani Ditt Singh.

In Amritsar, Bhai Vir Singh, the poet you met a few days ago, ran the Khalsa Samachar. They carried news, arguments about reform, explanations of Sikh history and practice, and appeals for schools and causes.
Third, the tracts: small, cheap booklets on single subjects, a Guru's life, the meaning of a hymn, how to hold a ceremony. Vir Singh helped found a society to publish them.
A tract could be bought for a coin, read in an evening, passed to a neighbor.
Fourth, why print mattered. The Gurus had gathered their hymns into a book so the word could be kept and shared.
Near the end of the Granth, Guru Arjan speaks of a dish holding truth, contentment and reflection, and Sikh tradition hears that dish as the Granth itself.
Print was another way of laying that dish out for everyone. A movement of a few learned men became a conversation in many households.
Arguments still broke out, sometimes fierce ones, but they broke out among people who were reading.

how: Sikh newspapers, magazines and publishers still print in Gurmukhi and English, and gurdwaras often keep free booklets on Sikh history and practice for visitors to take home.

games.why: reformers started Punjabi papers and tracts, and the paper traveled where they couldn't. print spreads it.

practice: Choose one Punjabi word you already know from this path, Waheguru, sangat, seva, langar or Khalsa, and picture it written in Gurmukhi, even if you don't know the letters: curved shapes hanging from a line at the top.
Breathe in and hear the word; breathe out and let it rest.

wordCard.voice: Akhbar, newspaper, a word Punjabi shares with Persian and Urdu: the Gurmukhi papers, presses and tracts that carried the reform into households across the Punjab. Today's word.
